PAPER: Case Report JHSMR Journal of Health Science and Medical Research Eight Weeks of Plyometric Training for a Professional Volleyball Athlete Four Months Post-Knee Arthroscopy and Bone Repair: A Case Report Chatanun Chinpeerasathian, P.T., Ph.D.1, Tibparat Kaewsai, P.T., B.Sc.2 1Department of Physical Therapy, Faculty of Allied Health Sciences, Chulalongkorn University, Pathum Wan, Bangkok 10330, Thailand. 2Thailand Volleyball Association, Bangkapi, Bangkok 10240, Thailand. Received 26 September 2024 l Revised 8 December 2024 l Accepted 12 January 2025 l Published online 8 May 2025 Abstract: Knee surgery can significantly diminish muscle strength, power, and vertical jump performance in athletes, particularly in volleyball athletes. Plyometric exercises are well-established for their efficacy in enhancing these physical attributes. This case report aimed to demonstrate the application of an 8-week plyometric exercise program to improve knee muscle strength, power, and vertical jump performance in a 20-year-old professional volleyball athlete, 4 months post-arthroscopic removal and repair of left knee osteophytes during the return-to-sport phase. The athlete, who was pain-free and had full knee range of motion at the program’s start, showed significant gains: quadriceps and hamstring strength increased by 42%-116% in the left knee and 31%-78% in the right knee, with power output rising up to 400%. Vertical jump performance also improved notably. These results suggest that plyometric training can effectively boost recovery and performance in athletes following knee surgery. JSON: Name: plyo_post_arthroscopy_volleyball Title: Efficacy of an 8-week progressive plyometric training program for improving knee isokinetic strength, power, and vertical jump performance in professional volleyball athletes four months after knee arthroscopy: a randomized controlled trial Short Hypothesis: An 8-week progressive plyometric training program initiated four months after knee arthroscopy causes greater increases in quadriceps and hamstring isokinetic peak torque and vertical jump height than a matched progressive resistance program or standard rehabilitation alone in professional volleyball athletes. Related Work: Existing rehabilitation literature demonstrates that structured progressive exercise improves post-operative knee strength and function, and systematic reviews indicate plyometric training can increase jump performance and neuromuscular power in athletes. Prior clinical studies have focused primarily on anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction or total knee arthroplasty populations, with limited evidence specific to arthroscopic osteophyte removal or multi-structural cartilage/bone repair. Reported limitations in current approaches include small sample sizes, single-arm case reports or non-randomized designs, inconsistent outcome sets (varying isokinetic velocities, differing jump tests), little investigation of sport-specific progressive plyometric protocols for return-to-play, unclear dose–response and phase-progression parameters, and limited safety/adverse-event reporting for high-intensity plyometrics in early post-operative return-to-sport phases. Abstract: Problem: Professional volleyball athletes frequently require arthroscopic knee procedures for osteophytes/loose bodies and cartilage repair; evidence is limited on sport-specific interventions to restore explosive knee strength and jump performance in the return-to-sport phase. Approach: We propose a randomized controlled trial comparing an 8-week, phase-progressive plyometric program to a matched progressive resistance program and standard rehabilitation in athletes at four months post-knee arthroscopy. Primary outcomes are isokinetic quadriceps peak torque (60 degrees/s) and countermovement vertical jump height. Secondary outcomes include isokinetic measures at 180 and 300 degrees/s, average power, H/Q ratio, single-leg hop, dynamic balance, patient-reported function and adverse events. Contribution: The study will quantify efficacy, dose-response, and safety of a volleyball-specific plyometric progression versus alternative rehabilitation approaches and provide standardized outcome benchmarks for return-to-sport decision-making. Expected outcome: We expect the plyometric program to produce greater improvements in explosive strength and vertical jump performance without an increased adverse-event rate, informing evidence-based post-arthroscopy sport-specific rehabilitation. Experiments: Design: prospective, assessor-blinded, three-arm randomized controlled trial with 1:1:1 allocation. Participants: professional or semi-professional volleyball athletes aged 18-30, 4.0 ± 0.5 months after unilateral knee arthroscopy with bone spur/loose body removal and cartilage/bone repair, pain-free at rest, full knee ROM, medical clearance for plyometrics. Exclusions: concomitant full-thickness grafts, staged procedures, systemic disease, prior contralateral knee surgery within 12 months, unresolved infection. Sample size: target n=90 (30 per arm) based on detecting Cohen's d=0.8 on primary outcome with alpha=0.05, power=0.80, and 15% dropout. Arms: (A) Progressive plyometric program (three-phase double-leg to single-leg progression matching the case-report progression and total weekly volume), (B) Matched progressive resistance training (heavy-load lower-limb strength program matched for session frequency and total work-time but without reactive plyometrics), (C) Standard rehabilitation (usual-care maintenance program for return-to-play). Outcomes and timepoints: baseline (pre-intervention), mid-intervention (end phase 2, ~week 5), post-intervention (week 8), 3-month follow-up, 6-month follow-up. Primary outcomes: isokinetic quadriceps peak torque at 60 deg/s (Nm and peak torque/BW) and countermovement vertical jump height (cm). Secondary outcomes: isokinetic measures at 180 and 300 deg/s (peak torque, average power), H/Q ratio, single-leg hop distance, Y-balance composite score, patient-reported outcomes (IKDC or KOOS subscales), pain VAS, time-to-return-to-sport, adverse events and re-injury incidence. Measurement protocols: Biodex isokinetic testing with standardized warm-up; velocities tested in randomized order to avoid velocity-order fatigue with minimum 2 minutes rest between velocities; vertical jump measured with Vertec and force-platform-derived jump metrics where available; blinded assessors. Baselines and monitoring: training load logged; adherence recorded; adverse events monitored by an independent safety officer. Statistical analysis: primary analysis by intention-to-treat using linear mixed-effects models with fixed effects for group, time, and group*time interaction and random intercepts for subjects; baseline covariates included if imbalanced. Pairwise comparisons: plyometric vs resistance, plyometric vs standard-care, resistance vs standard-care with Bonferroni correction. Report effect sizes (Cohen's d), 95% CIs, and p-values; significance threshold p<0.05. Ablation/comparison studies: predefined sub-study randomizing the plyometric arm participants to mini-trampoline warm-up inclusion vs exclusion to test component contribution (mini-trampoline ablation). Additional analyses: per-protocol analysis, dose–response modeling (total foot contacts vs outcomes), sensitivity analyses excluding participants with poor adherence. Data management: pre-registered protocol, centralized database, blinded data monitoring. Risk Factors and Limitations: Limited generalizability: results may not extend to non-volleyball athletes, older patients, or different types of knee surgery (e.g., ACL reconstruction). Recruitment feasibility: obtaining adequate numbers of professional athletes at the same post-op timepoint is challenging. Safety/reinjury risk: plyometric loading could provoke re-injury or cartilage symptoms despite screening; safety monitoring required. Measurement biases: isokinetic testing order and insufficient rest can cause fatigue and confound high-velocity measures; inter-device or inter-tester variability may affect reliability. Adherence and co-interventions: variable compliance and concurrent team training may confound treatment effects. Sample size assumptions: effect-size overestimation may lead to underpowered study. Blinding constraints: participants cannot be blinded to intervention, which may introduce expectancy/placebo effects. External validity: supervised clinical setting outcomes may differ from real-world team settings. Resource/scale limits: requirement for specialized equipment (Biodex, Vertec, force plates) and trained therapists limits scalability. Long-term outcomes: 6-month follow-up may be insufficient to capture late re-injury or osteoarthritis progression.
